editorNote: Acorn crosses the Atlantic with a school-minded BBC Micro package while compatibility disputes, lower-priced 16-bit challengers, and touch-screen ideas crowd the personal-computer desk.
morningLine: The BBC Micro arrives in America, Spectrum owners meet a compatibility snag, and the IBM-compatible field gets more crowded.

lead.headline: Britain's BBC Micro Makes Its American Debut
lead.dek: Acorn aims its $995 package at U.S. classrooms, with teacher notes, networking ambitions, and a 50,000-machine production commitment.
body: Acorn Computer brought one of Britain's best-known educational machines to the United States this week, formally unveiling an American BBC Micro package priced at $995. The October 7 debut placed the machine directly into the contest for school computer labs, where Apple and other established suppliers already had strong positions.

The American configuration was described as a beefed-up BBC Micro, with connections for disk storage, speech synthesis, and Acorn's Econet local-area network. Two sets of teacher-training notes came with the package, underscoring that Acorn was selling a classroom system and curriculum proposition rather than a bare home computer.

Popular Computing Weekly reported that Wong Electronics of Hong Kong had been commissioned to produce 50,000 U.S.-market machines over the next twelve months, with the first units due to ship during October. That production target gave the launch weight beyond a cautious export experiment, though schools remained the primary audience.

Acorn also planned to convene American education specialists to review domestic software, promote the strongest programs, and point developers toward gaps in the catalog. The company still hoped families would buy the machine for home use, but its first American argument was clear: computing belonged in the classroom, supported by software, training, and a network ready to link desks together.

stories.headline: Issue 3 Spectrum Change Breaks Some Existing Programs
stories.dek: Sinclair blames undocumented programming practices as cassette-era assumptions catch up with owners.
body: Owners of the new Issue 3 ZX Spectrum found that some programs written for earlier machines could fail because a replacement chip changed the byte describing the cassette and earphone port. Personal Computer News reported that software houses had not been warned before affected machines reached users.

Sinclair told dealers that programmers had relied on unsupported, undocumented behavior and called the practice unprofessional. Whatever the technical merits, customers were left holding software that had worked on yesterday's Spectrum but not necessarily today's—a sharp lesson in how fragile compatibility could be in the fast-growing cassette market.

stories.headline: Sanyo's $2,100 Challenger Joins the IBM-Compatible Charge
stories.dek: An 8088, twin drives, color output, and bundled DOS sharpen the price contest around the PC standard.
body: Sanyo's 555 arrived in reports from the SICOB show as another direct challenge to IBM's increasingly influential personal-computer platform. The 8088 system offered 128K of memory, two double-sided floppy drives, a Centronics printer connection, 16-color video output, MS-DOS, and Sanyo BASIC; CP/M-86 was optional.

Personal Computer News put the British price near £1,400, while an October BYTE dealer advertisement listed a dual-drive U.S. configuration at $2,095. The exact bundles differed, but the message was the same: manufacturers were assembling capable 16-bit DOS machines around an emerging standard and competing hard on included hardware and price.

stories.headline: Hewlett-Packard Puts 'Magic' at Your Fingertips
stories.dek: The HP 150 senses a finger through an infrared grid surrounding its screen.
body: BYTE's October cover previewed Hewlett-Packard's HP 150 under its development name, Magic. The 8088 desktop ran MS-DOS but was not hardware-compatible with the IBM PC, and its most striking feature was a screen that users could operate by touch.

Rather than relying on a pressure-sensitive display, the machine placed infrared emitters and detectors around the screen to locate an interrupting finger. Paired with still-unusual Sony 3.5-inch rigid-shell disks, the HP 150 offered a glimpse of a friendlier desktop interface—one that invited users to point directly at choices instead of memorizing every command.
